title: Buttons tell the truth
statement: A button tells the truth: it names what it does, never claims understanding or previews the next page, and when locked stays visible and says in words what unlocks it.
example: One lesson's Next sat padlocked for six screens with no reason given and no cue that it would unlock.
detail: A UI review of a Grade 3 reading lesson found a forward button labelled 'I know what to watch for', a claim the child cannot fail to make, so it asserted understanding without checking any, and a Next control padlocked for six screens with no reason given, which an eight-year-old reads as 'you are not allowed'. The course renamed the label to a plain 'Next page' and kept its reading and answer gates independent of it, and its repair shows the current action's status beside Back with a labelled held Next. Its QA checklist, under 'Buttons tell the truth', fails a locked forward control that vanishes or gives no reason, and its published rules bar a button that announces the next page's content.
against: The rule rests on one supplied review's judgment of how a child reads a padlock, not on observed learners. The final verification marks both the relabel and the explained lock implemented, but warns not to read that as full academic, listening, assistive-technology or every-possible-interaction acceptance (`grade3-reading/ui-audit-2026-09-08/round-5/final-standard-verification/ALADDIN-STANDARD-REVIEW.md`, lines 11, 41 and 57).
